claims.statement: `handlers::search::search` is a pure delegation to `repositories::search::search`, which accepts a `SearchQuery` (q plus optional category_id, container_id, source_type, page, size) and returns `SearchResult { items, total, page, size }` where each hit pairs an `ItemSummary` with an optional pre-rendered `highlight` string.
Both search SQL paths join `items`, so a leftover `items_fts` row whose item was deleted can neither appear in results nor inflate `total`.

Search pagination floors `page` at 1 (default 1), clamps `size` to the range 1..=100 (default 20), derives `offset` from them, and echoes the effective `page`/`size` back so a clamped request size is only observable in the response.

Query planning branches on `q.chars().count() < 3`: fewer than three characters uses the `LIKE` fallback, three or more uses `MATCH` on `items_fts`, and because the test counts characters rather than bytes two hanzi take the fallback while the trigram tokenizer's three-character floor makes the FTS path unusable for them.

The short-query fallback binds `%q%` six times over `i.name`, `i.description`, `i.location_note`, the immediate container's `name` and `label`, and the category `name` (via LEFT JOINs on `i.container_id` and `i.category_id`), orders by `i.created_at DESC`, and uses two hard-coded `0..6` bind loops whose literal count must be kept in sync with the WHERE clause.

The LIKE branch projects `NULL as name_snippet, NULL as desc_snippet` and no `note_snippet` column at all, while `SearchRow` declares three snippet fields with no `#[sqlx(default)]` annotation — so short-query rows are mapped against a result set missing a column the row type expects, making this the least-verified part of the subsystem and the thing to fix by aliasing `NULL as note_snippet`.

Because `q` is only trimmed and never validated for emptiness, `GET /search?q=` becomes `LIKE '%%'`, which matches every item (name is NOT NULL) and returns the entire inventory newest-first; the SPA avoids this only by disabling the query when `params.q.trim().length` is 0.

The FTS path wraps the query as a double-quoted phrase (`format!("\"{q}\"")`), which neutralises FTS5 operators (no prefix matching, OR, or column filters are reachable) but does not escape embedded double quotes, so a query containing `"` produces an unterminated FTS5 string whose sqlx error maps to `AppError::Internal` and a 500.

Each FTS hit carries `snippet(items_fts, 1|2|3, '<mark>', '</mark>', '…', 20|32|32)` and the list is ordered by `rank`, so `items_fts` column order is an API: columns 1-3 are addressed positionally as name, description, and location_note.

Search filters are assembled by one helper that seeds the clause with `1=1` and then appends `i.category_id = ?`, `i.container_id = ?`, `i.source_type = ?` in that fixed order, with binds following the same order in both the count and list statements; search has no tag filter and no filter on the FTS columns themselves.

Highlight assembly keeps only those snippets that contain `<mark>`, joins them in name, description, location-note order with `" … "`, and otherwise falls back to the item's description truncated to 80 characters plus `…` (or null when there is no description); since `snippet()` is per column, a row that matched only in `tags`, `container_name`, `container_label`, or `category_name` produces no marked fragment and therefore no highlight.

The container breadcrumb is not read from `items_fts`: after rows are fetched, each hit with a `container_id` calls `container::get_path`, which issues one query per ancestor level, so a results page costs one query per hit times its container depth.

The frontend renders `highlight` as trusted HTML via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` behind a truthiness guard, so the `<mark>` markers and any user-entered item text inside the snippet are interpreted as markup — the fragment is escaped nowhere on either side.

On the client, `q` and `page` live in the URL (coerced by `validateSearch`, rewritten on submit, changed by paging links) and `useSearch` keys a TanStack Query on the full params object; only item create/update/delete invalidate `["search"]`, while tag, container, and category mutations invalidate their own lists and never the search query.

`items_fts` is maintained only by `services/search_index.rs` plus one raw statement in the item delete handler — there are no triggers and no external-content declaration: item create and update handlers call `sync_item` after the repository has written `item_tags`, item delete issues `DELETE FROM items_fts WHERE item_id = ?` directly in the handler, and `main.rs` calls `sync_all` between `db::init` and binding the router with failures reduced to a `tracing::warn`.

`sync_item` is a delete-then-insert of a single index row that re-derives every indexed field from the source tables on each call, is not transactional (an error between the two statements leaves the item unindexed rather than duplicated), and returns `Ok(())` when the item no longer exists — making it the safe repair primitive and the reason `sync_all`, which truncates the table and loops `sync_item` over every item id, is the only bulk rebuild path.

The indexed text is the item's `name`, `description`, and `location_note`, its space-joined tag names, the immediate container's `name` and `label`, and the category `name`; ancestor container names and the purchase fields (`purchased_at`, `bought_from`, `price`) are never indexed or matched, so an item is not findable by the room above its box.

Drift is structural, not accidental: tag rename/delete, container rename/label change/delete, and category rename/delete all write rows that `items_fts` folded into its text but issue no FTS statement, so old strings stay searchable and new strings stay invisible until the next process start runs `sync_all`; the LIKE fallback is unaffected because it reads live tables, and any new write path that changes indexed text must call `sync_item` for the linked items itself.

Because the list query joins `categories` live while the indexed copy of `category_name` is stale, one hit can display the new category name (and breadcrumb) while still matching the old indexed text — the displayed and matched values can disagree until a resync.

Adding a searchable field requires five coupled edits — a migration that drops and recreates `items_fts` with the new column, the `sync_item` INSERT list plus its gathering queries, an added `snippet()` call at the new positional index, the LIKE fallback's count and list WHERE clauses together with the hard-coded `0..6` bind loops, and no change to `sync_all` — and all tunables (tokenizer, snippet sizes and tokens, `<mark>` markers, ellipsis, page defaults, three-character threshold) are hard-coded rather than configurable.

There are no automated tests covering search or the index (AGENTS.md records `server/tests/` as empty), so verification is manual: comparing `COUNT(*)` between `items` and `items_fts`, inspecting one item's indexed `tags`/`container_name`/`category_name` for drift forensics, and probing the same term at two and three characters to cross the LIKE/FTS boundary.
